## Findings by module

### 5

- **confirmed** (ch-050 chunk 1 (government: Alafin, Oyo Mesi, Basorun, Aremo)): Johnson (1890s, from Oyo court tradition): Yoruba Proper was an 'absolute monarchy' yet the king is elected from the royal family by the seven Oyo Mesi, with the Basorun's voice paramount; the heir (Aremo) had to die with his father, a rule repealed in 1858; accession needs a three-month seclusion, a visit to the Bara royal tomb, crowning at Sango's shrine, and the great sword brought from Ife; vassal and provincial rulers numbered 1,060 at the empire's height, which included the Popos, Dahomey and parts of Ashanti (Johnson's claim, high and partisan). Confirms the course's Oyo Mesi and Bashorun checks on the Alafin (Module 5 lesson 3); Johnson calls it absolute monarchy, which sits against Reader's point that kingship was often a cycle; the 1,060 figure and the Ashanti claim are [THIN EVIDENCE].
- **confirmed** (ch-050 chunk 4 (the seven Oyo Mesi, the Basorun, the Eso and the Kakanfo)): Johnson: seven hereditary councillors, the Oyo Mesi (Basorun, Agbakin, Samu, Alapini, Laguna, Akiniku, Asipa), who elect the king and speak for the nation; the Basorun can move the king's rejection, in which case the king must take poison and die, an 'unwritten constitution of checks and counter-checks'; Basorun families in five lines, one so powerful it outlived kings; a second class of military nobles, the Eso, rank by merit, seventy captains in all, headed by the Kakanfo (field-marshal, introduced under an early king). Confirms the course's Oyo Mesi, Bashorun and cavalry-state description in Module 5 lesson 3; Johnson's suicide rule and the 1858 abolition are his account, and the Basorun's power over kings fits Reader's and Rodney's view of Oyo's overextension.
- **refined** (ch-056 chunk 2 (the 1,060 vassal kings)): Johnson's number of 1,060 vassal kings appears in his government chapter as the empire's peak count and again in a legend where Ajaka puts all 1,060 to death and their skulls become a cult object; the figure is a legendary number in both places, so it must not be quoted as an Oyo statistic. Johnson also reads Yoruba legends as 'garbled' Bible stories, a 1890s missionary frame the course does not share.
- **extended** (ch-047 chunk 1 (Johnson on origins: Lamurudu, Oduduwa, Oranyan)): Johnson (written by 1897): court historians of Oyo, hereditary families who were also bards and drummers, are his sources, and he warns their accounts vary. Tradition: Oduduwa, son of king Lamurudu of 'Mecca', fled after a religious civil war and settled at Ile-Ife; his grandchildren became the kings of Owu, Ketu, Benin, Ila, Sabe, Popo and Oranyan (Oyo); Oranyan, left only the land, became lord of the land (Alafin l'oni ile), with a second version where a cock scatters earth on the water and 21 pieces of iron are his share; Oranyan founded Oyo Ajaka by following a boa constrictor; the Alafin, Alake and Owa are installed with a sword brought from Ife. Johnson himself doubts Mecca but argues the Yoruba came from Upper Egypt or Nubia as followers of Nimrod, citing Ife 'Egyptian marbles' and a Phoenician-looking obelisk: that is his own 1890s diffusionist inference and the course rejects the Egypt and Phoenicia claims, as it rejects Frobenius [CONTESTED]. Gives Module 5 lesson 4 a second Ife-Oduduwa variant (Mecca and Oranyan) beside Woodson's tale.
- **extended** (ch-047 chunk 2 (Ife priest Oni, four Oyo provinces, 19th-century changes)): Johnson: the high priest of Ife (the Oni, from Adimu, 'son of a sacrificial victim') kept the national gods while the capital moved to Oyo; new Oyo kings must send to Oduduwa's grave and receive Oranyan's sword from Ife; Oyo's heartland had four provinces (Ekun Otun, Ekun Osi, Ibolo, Epo); 19th-century wars destroyed Old Oyo, shifted its name to Ago Oja, and made Ibadan the leading town while the Egba gathered from 153 hamlets into Abeokuta. The Ife-Oyo ritual link supports Module 5 lessons 1 and 3; the 19th-century counts are Johnson's, writing in the 1890s.
- **extended** (ch-048 chunk 1 (origin of the tribes: Ife as source, Oyo tribute, Egba, Ijebu, Ijesa)): Johnson: all Yoruba kingdoms trace descent from Oduduwa and Ife, and rulers prove legitimacy by a link to the Alafin of Oyo; Dahomey and Popo paid regular tribute to Oyo (as Rodney and Reader also say for Dahomey); Egba lived in 153 hamlets without a king until forced together in the 19th-century wars; Awujale of Ijebu said to descend from an Oyo envoy (ilari); Ijesa origin stories (food of the gods) are folk etymologies Johnson calls myths. Shows how origin traditions work as political charters (Module 5 lesson 4 myth checklist) and confirms Oyo's tributary reach (Module 5 lesson 3). Johnson's ethnic characterisations (Ijesa, Ijebu) are 1890s prejudice and are not used.
- **extended** (ch-050 chunks 2-3 (festivals, funerals, palace offices)): Johnson: three annual royal festivals (Ifa, Orun, Bere) in which the Basorun and king perform rites together; the king ritually 'reviewed' by the Basorun's kola divination (if unfavourable he must die); royal burial in the Bara with immolations (abolished, he says, in his time); officials 'to die with the king' (Aremo, master of the horse and others); palace staff of eunuchs (Iwefa), Ilari body guards, executioners (Tetu), rhapsodist-historians (Arokin), and a women's hierarchy with the king's official mother (Iya Oba) and the Iya kere controlling the royal insignia. Rich detail on Oyo's court from an insider but the sacrifice counts are from oral memory and a missionary-era author; use only the structure (council, ritual checks, eunuchs, women officials) for Module 5 lesson 3 and tag figures [THIN EVIDENCE].
- **extended** (ch-050 chunk 5 (Kakanfo, vassal kings, Ogboni among the Egba and Ijebu)): Johnson: the Kakanfo, a field-marshal created outside the capital and bound to fight a campaign every three years; vassal kings take titles and the sword of justice from the Alafin, and each important town keeps an official at Oyo; but among the Egba and Ijebu the Ogboni (Osugbo) councils are the real executive with power of life and death, and 'Egbas have no king that rules', while in the Oyo provinces the Ogboni only advise. A usable contrast for Module 5 lessons 3 and 4: one Yoruba people with a strongly checked monarchy and neighbours governed by councils. Written from 1890s memory of the pre-war order.
- **extended** (ch-056 chunk 1 (Johnson on Oduduwa, Oranyan, Sango, Ajaka)): Johnson himself writes that Oduduwa 'is really a mythical personage' and explains the name from Ife theology (sent from heaven to create the earth, wife Olokun); Oranyan is the founder of Oyo, with a stone obelisk (Opa Oranyan) at Ife that Johnson says was about 10 to 12 feet tall and lost its top in 1884, with 61 and 31 nails he reads as ages; Sango is a fire-breathing early Alafin who unified Oyo and died by hanging, later worshipped as the god of thunder; Ajaka is deposed and recalled; the Moremi legend tells of Ife raided by masked 'Igbo' people. Johnson's story of Oyo's moving its capital and the Alafin being checked by the Oyo Mesi (Ajaka confirmed in Oranyan's absence) supports the lesson's 'myth as political charter' and the checked-monarchy picture. His reading of the nails as Phoenician letters is outdated [THIN EVIDENCE].

Totals: 2 confirmed, 1 refined, 0 contradicted, 6 extended, 0 absent, 0 note.
